title: Improved Vision Through Gaming: Brain Imaging Shows That Playing Action Video Games Sharpens Peripheral Sight
content: The human visual system is characterized by a sophisticated, parallel processing architecture that begins in the retina and extends through the thalamus to the primary visual cortex and higher-order extrastriate regions. This architecture is fundamentally divided into two major functional streams, the magnocellular (M) and parvocellular (P) pathways. These pathways are not merely redundant transmission lines, but are specialized to handle distinct aspects of visual information, effectively allowing the brain to parse the environment into dynamic spatial frameworks and detailed object identities. The magnocellular pathway is optimized for the detection of motion, depth, and large-scale spatial contrast in the peripheral visual field, whereas the parvocellular pathway is specialized for high-resolution detail and color recognition in the central visual field. Action games, often questioned for their potentially detrimental effects on various human capacities, are here hypothesized to strengthen the magnocellular pathway in particular, which is due to their heavy peripheral field engagement. Twenty-five participants (13 gamers/12 non-gamers) were recruited to participate and get their brain activities recorded during passive viewing of four very simple visual presentations on black background (left white circle, right white circle, simultaneous left and right white circles (bilateral peripheral), and central white circle). In random order, each of these stimuli were presented 50 times for 300ms each. Most interestingly, the mean latency of the N2-ERP component for the condition, in which a left and a right stimulus were presented simultaneously in gamers was 237.77ms, whereas it was 263.36ms in non-gamers. This latency difference turned out statistically significant. On the other hand, the condition, where only one stimulus was presented in the center, did not lead to different latencies (mean latency for gamers was 170.96ms (P170) and for non-gamers it was 165.18ms. It is concluded that gamers show faster processing of bilateral peripheral stimulation than non-gamers, whereas central stimulation leads to comparable processing latencies in both groups.
